Our best protection from all of those risks might be using CTI software to ratify a World Constitution that is based on the principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Earth Charter.
Laws are passed by elected representatives. Supreme laws are approved by referendums with direct votes by the people, whether it's at the local, state, national, or global level.
Ratification of the principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Earth Charter by a global referendum would give those principles the force of supreme law for all nations.

The International Court of Justice can rule on disputes between states, but its judgments are only enforced if the Security Council chooses to act. A court whose rulings depend on the goodwill of the parties is not a court in the ordinary sense.
Most states have never accepted the International Court of Justice's compulsory jurisdiction, and several that once did have since withdrawn. International law binds only those who agree to be bound.
Global rules can be enforced without a world government. The Montreal Protocol phased out ozone depleting chemicals through trade measures and a funding mechanism, and nearly every country complied.

Any one of the five permanent members can block a Security Council resolution, whatever the rest of the world thinks. Since 1946 the veto has been used hundreds of times, often to shield the member casting it or its allies.

The General Assembly can act when the Council is blocked. The Uniting for Peace resolution of 1950 lets the Assembly recommend collective measures, and since 2022 the Assembly meets within ten days of any veto to debate it.

A carbon tax approved by a global referendum would be supreme law for all nations. The referendum would specify how the carbon tax money, $1 trillion per year for instance, would be spent. If the damages caused by greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels was less than $1 trillion per year, the remainder could be spent on financing the transition to solar, wind, battery, and other technologies to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions.

National climate pledges under the Paris Agreement are voluntary, and the gap between what countries have promised and what the science requires has not closed. Without a body that can set and enforce a shared limit, each country has a reason to wait for the others.

Carbon pricing now exists in dozens of countries, but it covers only about a quarter of global emissions and most prices are far below what would be needed to meet the Paris goals. A single global price would remove the incentive to move pollution across borders.
No global body is directly elected. The General Assembly represents governments, not people, and a citizen of a large democracy has no more say in it than the ruler of a small dictatorship.
Estonia shows that a whole country can vote, sign and govern online with a trusted digital identity. The tools for direct participation at a large scale already exist.

Who has control now? The higher, the fewer. Autonomy requires controls, rules, and laws. I would like to see the principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Earth Charter ratified as supreme law for all nations.
